questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2x}{{y}^{2}}$ that satisfies $y(2)=\sqrt[3]{13}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find the particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2x}{{y}^{2}} \\ {y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x \\ \int {y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ \int {y}^{2}\,\text{d}y & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{{y}^{3}}{3} & ={x}^{2}+{C}_{1} \\ {y}^{3} & =3{x}^{2}+3{C}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the general solution is

$$
{y}^{3}=3{x}^{2}+C,
$$

where $C=3{C}_{1}$  is an arbitrary constant.

We now apply the condition $y(2)=\sqrt[3]{13}$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\sqrt[3]{13})}^{3} & =3(2)^{2}+C \\ 13 & =12+C \\ C & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2x}{{y}^{2}}$ that satisfies the condition $y(2)=\sqrt[3]{13}$ is

$$
{y}^{3}=3{x}^{2}+1.
$$

questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}$ that satisfies $y(0)=0.$ Assume that $-\frac{\pi }{4}<y<\frac{\pi }{4}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)} \\ (\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x) \\ \int (\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)\,\text{d}y & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2y) & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+C \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2y) & =-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+{C}_{1}\,,\end{aligned}
$$

where ${C}_{1}=2C.$

We now apply the condition $y(0)=0$ to find ${C}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot 0) & =-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot 0)+{C}_{1} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(0) & =-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+{C}_{1} \\ 0 & =-\frac{2}{3}\cdot 1+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

So we get the particular solution in implicit form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2y) & =\frac{2}{3}-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the above equation as

$$
3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2y)=2(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)).
$$

questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡y}$ that satisfies $y(0)=\frac{\pi }{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find the particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡y} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \int \operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡y & =x+C \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡y & =-x-C.\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the condition $y(0)=\frac{\pi }{2}$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-0-C \\ 0 & =0-C \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So we get the particular solution in implicit form:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡y=-x
$$

questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{y}^{2}=0$ that satisfies $y(1)=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find the particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{y}^{2} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-{y}^{2} \\ -\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ -\int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{y} & =x+C \\ y & =\frac{1}{x+C}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the general solution is

$$
y=\frac{1}{x+C},
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now apply the condition $y(1)=1$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =\frac{1}{1+C} \\ 1+C & =1 \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{y}^{2}=0$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=1$ is

$$
y=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=4x\sqrt{y}$
that satisfies the condition $y(1)=9.$  Assume that $y>0.$

We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find the particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4x\sqrt{y} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\,\text{d}y & =4x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\,\text{d}y & =\int 4x\,\text{d}x \\ 2\sqrt{y} & =2{x}^{2}+{C}_{1} \\ \sqrt{y} & ={x}^{2}+\frac{{C}_{1}}{2} \\ y & ={({x}^{2}+\frac{{C}_{1}}{2})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Assuming $y>0,$ the general solution is

$$
y(x)=({x}^{2}+C)^{2},
$$

where $C=\frac{{C}_{1}}{2}$ is an arbitrary constant.

$$
\begin{aligned}9 & =((1)^{2}+C)^{2} \\ 9 & =(1+C)^{2} \\ 3 & =1+C \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution is

$$
y(x)=({x}^{2}+2)^{2}.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-4x\sqrt{x} & =3 \\ \sqrt{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3+4x\sqrt{x} \\ \text{d}y & =(3{x}^{-1/2}+4x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \text{d}y & =\int (3{x}^{-1/2}+4x)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =6{x}^{1/2}+2{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the initial condition $y(1)=11$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =11 \\ 6(1)^{1/2}+2(1)^{2}+C & =11 \\ C+8 & =11 \\ C & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =6{x}^{1/2}+2{x}^{2}+3 \\  & =6\sqrt{x}+2{x}^{2}+3.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-4x{y}^{2} & =4x \\ 2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4x{y}^{2}+4x \\ 2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4x({y}^{2}+1) \\ \frac{2y}{{y}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}y & =4x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{2y}{{y}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}y & =\int 4x\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+1) & =2{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Exponentiating both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+1)} & ={e}^{2{x}^{2}+C} \\ {y}^{2}+1 & =C{e}^{2{x}^{2}} \\ y & =\sqrt{C{e}^{2{x}^{2}}-1}\end{aligned}
$$

where we used that $y>0.$

We now apply the initial condition $y(0)=1$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =1 \\ \sqrt{C{e}^{2(0)^{2}}-1} & =1 \\ \sqrt{C-1} & =1 \\ C-1 & =1 \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution is

$$
y(x)=\sqrt{2{e}^{2{x}^{2}}-1}.
$$

questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=3{y}^{2}{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}{x}^{3}$ that satisfies $y(2)=\frac{1}{8}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{y}^{2}{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}{x}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={y}^{2}(3{x}^{2}-4{x}^{3}) \\ \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}-4{x}^{3} \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (3{x}^{2}-4{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y & =3\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x-4\int {x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{y} & ={x}^{3}-{x}^{4}+C \\ y & =\frac{1}{{x}^{4}-{x}^{3}-C}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the initial condition $y(2)=\frac{1}{8}$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(2) & =\frac{1}{8} \\ \frac{1}{{2}^{4}-{2}^{3}-C} & =\frac{1}{8} \\ \frac{1}{8-C} & =\frac{1}{8} \\ C & =0\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=3{y}^{2}{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}{x}^{3}$ that satisfies the condition $y(2)=\frac{1}{8}$ is

$$
y=\frac{1}{{x}^{4}-{x}^{3}}\,.
$$

questions.problem: Find the specific solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x+y}$ given that  $\,y(0)=-\operatorname{ln}⁡2.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{x+y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{x}{e}^{y} \\ {e}^{-y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{x} \\ \int {e}^{-y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{-y}\,\text{d}y & =\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\ -{e}^{-y} & ={e}^{x}+{C}_{1} \\ {e}^{-y} & =-{e}^{x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-y}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(-{e}^{x}+C) \\ -y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(C-{e}^{x}) \\ y & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡(C-{e}^{x}).\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the condition $y(0)=-\operatorname{ln}⁡2$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡(C-{e}^{0}) & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(C-1) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ C-1 & =2 \\ C & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x+y}$ that satisfies the condition $y(0)=-\operatorname{ln}⁡2$ is

$$
y=-\operatorname{ln}⁡(3-{e}^{x}).
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{-x-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{-x}{e}^{-y} \\ {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{-x} \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int {e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x \\ {e}^{y} & =-{e}^{-x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{y}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(-{e}^{-x}+C) \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(-{e}^{-x}+C).\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the condition $y(0)=-\operatorname{ln}⁡4$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡4 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(-{e}^{0}+C) & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡4 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(C-1) & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡4 \\ C-1 & =\frac{1}{4} \\ C & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{-x-y}$ that satisfies the condition $y(0)=-\operatorname{ln}⁡4$ is

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{5}{4}-{e}^{-x}).
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $y' = 5y$ that satisfies $y(0)=3.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution, and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =5y \\ \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =5 \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =5\int \,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =5\int \,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =5x+C\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the exponential function to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\pm {e}^{5x+C} \\  & =\pm {e}^{C}{e}^{5x} \\  & =K{e}^{5x}\,,\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\pm e^{C}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

Now we apply the condition $y(0) = 3$ to find $K\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =3 \\ K{e}^{5\cdot 0} & =3 \\ K & =3\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $y' = 5y$ that satisfies the condition $y(0)=3$ is

$$
y = 3 e^{5x}  \,.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\cos(3y)\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} + \sin(2x) = 0$ given that  $y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 0.$ Assume that $-\dfrac{\pi}{6} < y < \dfrac{\pi}{6} .$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution, and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) \\ \int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3y)\,\text{d}y & =-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3y) & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+C \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3y) & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+{C}_{1}\,,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C_1=3C.$

Now let's apply the condition $y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 0$ to find $C_1\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot 0) & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})+{C}_{1} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(0) & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+{C}_{1} \\ 0 & =0+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So we get the particular solution in implicit form:

$$
\sin(3y)   =  \dfrac {3} {2} \cos(2x)
$$
